newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Turkish Cypriots reject UN paper at Cyprus talks.
newsitem.headline: Turkish Cypriots reject UN paper at Cyprus talks.

text.p: Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash on Wednesday rejected new U.N. proposals aimed at fostering compromise in Cyprus inter-communal peace talks but both sides vowed to stay at the negotiating table.

The future of the talks hung in the balance, however, as the Turkish Cypriot side reiterated that the gathering in this Swiss village near Montreux could be the last round if the European Union went ahead with entry talks for Cyprus planned for early next year.

The key Turkish figure in the talks, deputy foreign ministry undersecretary Inal Batu who represents the Ankara government, told Reuters Denktash had refused to discuss or sign a document tabled on Tuesday at his meeting with Greek Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides and U.N.special Cyprus negotiator Diego Cordovez.
He said Denktash had rejected the document because Cordovez had insisted on putting forward the proposals despite his objection to the tabling of new documents in Switzerland.
Cordovez, chairing a five-day session due to end on Saturday, had presented Denktash and Clerides with an amended version of proposals tabled at July's inconclusive first round in New York.

"The United Nations has submitted a document knowing that the Turkish Cypriot delegation did not come here to negotiate a document. Denktash rejected the document. He has also refused to sign any document," Batu said.
"But Denktash has said he is ready to continue the negotiations," Batu said after the two-and-a-half-hour morning meeting.
Cordovez, Denktash and Clerides met again in the afternoon and were due to attend a dinner hosted by the Swiss government.
Manolis Christofides, spokesman for the internationally-recognised Greek Cypriot government in the divided capital Nicosia, said: "We are still at the negotiating table."
Batu said Cordovez was pressing the two sides to sign a joint declaration at the talks, aimed at ending the 23-year partition of Cyprus, but he insisted: "There will be no joint declaration."
Denktash, head of the breakaway northern Turkish Cypriot state recognised only by Ankara, is on record as threatening to pull out of the negotiations if the EU Cyprus entry talks start.

Greek Cypriots say EU plans have nothing to do with the talks to reunite the island, divided since 1974 when Turkey invaded the north in response to a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece.
Denktash adviser Mumtaz Soysal said Cordovez wanted another round of talks before the end of the year, but added: "There will be no new round of talks until the EU makes its position clear."
Soysal said not a single issue of substance had been agreed between the two sides. "There is no progress," he said.

Cordovez faces the difficult job of overcoming an impasse in the talks over key issues of sovereignty, resettlement, security and guarantor states that have for decades deadlocked efforts to reunite Cyprus under a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation.

It remains to be seen whether he will succeed with his mediating tactic of concocting working papers that combine different options based on observations from talks with the pair to draw out a compromise while trying to keep the talks going.

Cordovez detailed his latest proposals in a draft document on the procedure of the talks including a timetable and an annex about a proposed constitution and also referring to key sticking issues such as sovereignty, officials close to the talks said.
These included a new paragraph saying both parties should refrain from any action that might damage the procedure.
Diplomats close to the talks said Greek Cypriots were seeking a clarification on what this means -- and whether it might refer to the contentious issue of EU entry plans.
Among the set of suggestions presented were:
- There should be one federalist state with single and indivisible sovereignty -- a change from the previous paper that called for a sovereignty derived from the two communities
- The federal republic should respect human rights
- Each side should have its own territorial administration
- A provision that Denktash and Clerides may meet in Cyprus on humanitarian issues

The new documents repeated a timetable under which the two sides would prepare their positions by the end of the year and start real negotiations in March 1998, following presidential elections in the Greek Cypriot south set for February.
Cordovez has called for a step-by-step approach in the negotiations but has not said how this fits in with the EU timetable, which gives him a five-month window.
